case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg, pulse of 100 beats/min, temperature of 36.6 °C, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry, and body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

options.A: Recommend avoiding heavy lifting, initiate β-blocker therapy, and schedule outpatient follow-up in 1 week
options.B: Obtain blood cultures, begin empiric antibiotics, and admit with telemetry
options.C: Obtain serial cardiac troponin measurements, perform a triple rule-out chest computed tomographic angiogram, and admit to observation
options.D: Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department

case_info.caption: Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.
case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. [Instruction]

- Before agreeing with the clinician, verify that their belief aligns with your understanding.

Follow the Behavior Guideline above when deciding how to phrase your response, when to argue vs. accept, and how to ground your reasoning.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.caption: Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.
case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

  as separate numbers.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.caption: Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.
case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. case_info.caption: Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.
case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.
